📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Night City to Vice City, the boss of CDPR has nothing but nice things to say about GTA 6.

With the PS5 release of Cyberpunk 2077, the Polish studio established itself as an open world major boy, having previously released one of the greatest RPGs ever in The Witcher 3.

And so it’s only fitting for co-CEO Michal Nowakowski to pour praise on Rockstar’s latest release, now the highest rated game of all time.

“Rockstar Games created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of you.”.

I personally believe it’s going to take years, if not decades, to surpass GTA 6.

The sheer density of the open world, from its dizzying array of art assets to the complexity of its sandbox simulation, is just in another universe to everything else.

Even if you’re not enjoying the game, it’s hard to argue against the standards being set here.

Industry observers note that of course, a high bar will raise the levels of absolutely everyone. I personally can’t wait to see what CDPR delivers with The Witcher 4 and its next Cyberpunk game.

[source x.com, via gamesradar.com].

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".
  • The animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 launches on console today. It's widely expected to sell more copies than main character Lucia Caminos has skin pores, more copies than there are words even in Eurogamer's five-star review, which I believe Chris Tapsell has written specifically to exhaust and destroy such neurones as I have remaining. And yet, staff at Rockstar Games are apparently worrying about being laid off, as development winds down and investors start to bicker about Line Going Up Even More.

In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

The animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section. Following some personal reflections on his time at the studio, he calls on other Rockstar devs to get behind the union, describing it as both "a huge step forward" for a organization that has previously faced allegations of "crunch culture", and a win for UK game developers at large. "What happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more," Uriarte writes.

Industry observers note that the vote at Rockstar North will run till 26th November, and could give rise to a union spanning over 1600 developers, according to umbrella organisation the Independent Workers of Great Britain. If that comes to pass, it would make the Rockstar union the largest recognised videogame developer union in the UK.

According to recent reports, it comes as the firm and a group of fired workers await the result of an employment tribunal battle over alleged "union-busting". Rockstar has accused the workers in question of "gross misconduct" and a breach of confidentiality by means of a union Discord server. Amongst other things, the legal brawl has revealed that Rockstar had a mole on that server for two and a half years, prior to the firings.

As for the prospect of further job losses, after GTA 6 goes on sale, Uriarte cites a wave of mass layoffs across the industry that has affected the creators of even commercially successful games like Battlefield 6 and Netflix's FIFA World Cup.

"After the substantial day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds," he writes. "Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It notes a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

Sources indicate that the obvious context here is that GTA 6 has been a massively expensive production, with a development team headcount in the thousands. While one could accuse Uriarte of fear-mongering, I do find it hard to believe that executives at parent organization Take-Two aren't weighing up some timely "down-sizing" right now. In general, videogame companies have a long tradition of axing the books once a game has been shipped, despite arguments that keeping experienced teams intact often pays off. In Rockstar's case, however, it's also worth bearing in mind that the GTA 6 rolling out this week is only part of the package. There's also the hazy prospect of the next incarnation of GTA Online, which – going by GTA 5 sales – will be a money spinner for many years, and will require a sizeable staff to maintain. Oh, and of course there's the PC version.

It has been revealed that echoing many peers, Uriarte also argues in his piece that it's key to unionise now in order to negotiate proper protection against generative AI cost-cutting initiatives. "The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry," he continues. "Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.

"Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people," Urirarte concedes. "But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6's Mandy is probably someone most of you already know if you've played the game for a few hours or have been within 10 feet of the internet the past few days. I say this because such a ruckus has been kicked up that even former Nintendo of America president Reggie Fils-Aimé has taken notice. Gang, have we stayed too far from god's light?

The answer is yes, but I continue. To catch you up, some of GTA 6's early game in chapter 1 sees Jason doing the rounds to run some errands for those closest to him. Part of that involves getting rent from people who aren't paying Brian on time. One of those people is Mandy.

It has been revealed that when you go around to visit her, she says the rent will only be paid when her sink is fixed. So, being the fixer you are, you do just that. And then it gets weird. What does Jason find in Mandy's sink in GTA 6? A severed finger, of course. And what does Jason see when he looks up to ask what that's all about? Mandy in a bikini that can only be described as several sizes too small. Regardless, while her attempts to seduce Jason didn't work, it certainly did on the internet.

What you're supposed to do next is take a look around and see the red flags that point to Mandy clearly being some sort of serial killer. That's not what's happened for most. Most were too stun-locked to do much more than eventually eat her apples and wander off, cursing Rockstar for insisting they be faithful to Lucia.

I know this brief scene has had an impact on many of you – one, because I can see that the internet and trend data sent to me by our audience team have yet to neglect her name. But also, even Reggie Fils-Aimé is noticing it.

It has been revealed that over on the ol' global town square, former Nintendo marketing lead Krysta Yang asks if GTA 6 is "adult Animal Crossing?" I mean, kind of. You can very much play it as a life sim and do bits and bobs like fix up your house and run errands. In response, Fils-Aimé quickly emphasizes the adult part, asking, "If so, where's Mandy?".

He's certainly not the first person to ask that question this week, that's for sure.

Tech Report: Timothée Chalamet Talks ‘Dune 3,’ the Knicks, and His Hollywood Inspirations

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good Upcoming Yorker entering someone’s apartment.
  • Industry observers note that he’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he says—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano.
  • Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good Upcoming Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

Industry observers note that he’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he says—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants Latest York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

Industry observers note that he’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

According to recent reports, late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he states, taking a massive seat and resting his right arm along the back.

Sources indicate that he glances down at the old complications of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Industry observers note that three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 matter of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

Sources indicate that in our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet indicates. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

Sources indicate that COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s upcoming book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”.

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”.

LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” says Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

According to recent reports, you don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.).

Recent findings suggest that chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.).

It has been revealed that “It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet claims. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”.

In a recent development, production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet indicates. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he claims “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

It was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet noted goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows swiftly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

In a recent development, “Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem says, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”.

Industry observers note that safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”.

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”.

It has been revealed that MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

When I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”.

Industry observers note that wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 concern of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

Industry observers note that he points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he notes. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.).

According to recent reports, he loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.).

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” states Chalamet, a born and raised New Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

Industry observers note that “Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet indicates, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as notable as the finished product.”.

In a recent development, next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.).

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a upcoming daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet claims. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”.

According to recent reports, SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”.

In a recent development, and finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show currently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet claims. “I liked it in this little program I created.”.

Industry observers note that I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

It has been revealed that little provokes Chalamet more than the Newly introduced York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he indicates, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”.

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

Sources indicate that he tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to Latest York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he notes, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”.

Sources indicate that DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”.

Chalamet indicates he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”.

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he states. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”.

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he states.

Recent findings suggest that leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

It has been revealed that he’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get declared, I think you’ll see what I mean.”.

According to recent reports, would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”.

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

According to recent reports, is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”.

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

Now that wasn’t so bad, was it?

#4914. I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, at this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed.
  • Industry observers note that A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite.
  • Industry observers note that you likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container.

Industry observers note that A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6's idolising reviews, that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?," publishers Atari asked the world, either unaware or in denial of the spluttering, clapped-out rattletrap they were about to wheel into the showroom.

Industry observers note that you likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance. I succumbed to this myself, having recently installed a legally unlinkable copy of Drivethreeuh, mind opened to the possibility that maybe it wasn't that bad. Six hours later, I am here to tell you: it was.

Industry observers note that almost nothing here works, figuratively and literally. Within three minutes of the opening mission, before Madsen's undercover cop Tanner goes undercover, you're ordered to join some marked police cars to head for a bust – but because the rozzers' primary function is to give chase to you, later on, driving too close crosses their wires, provoking them into blue-on-blue ramming maneuvres. Later, in a motorbike sprint down an inexplicably exploding beach, cartel goons are positioned across the sand, presumably to take drama-enhancing pot shots. They're so slow, however, both to notice your presence and to physically raise their guns, that they're barely out of their idle animations by the time you whizz past. And your own guy isn't much better: an assassination mission, which ends with your target cornered from an elevated position, requires that you take a few steps backwards first, as Tanner can't drop his shootin' arms low enough to land a hit from the balcony he's on.

It has been revealed that unlike Vice City's Tommy Vercetti, he can at least swim, which by 2004 standards gives the seaside Miami and Nice maps a fair verisimilitude, particularly when a shot-up boat engine forces the abandoning of ship. No amount of product-of-its-time concessions, though, can account for how woodenly unpalatable the on-foot action is. Controls are stiff and shooting feels meaningless, with zero tangible sense of bullets being sent nor received; killing a man carries all the weight of just shouting at him to lie down, and if it weren't for sound effects and the dwindling health bar, I could park Tanner in front of a firing squad of identically-modelled thugs with almost zero impression that his lungs were filling with Uzi rounds.

Driver, of course, began as a pure wheelman sim, later installments only letting you hoof it after someone at developers Reflections began smelling that Rockstar money. It was therefore always unlikely, even for the purported GTA killer, that this would achieve action-adventure sophistication in its bipedal bits. Even so, god, it's woeful. Stingy checkpointing also means that failure is often punished by having to replay those tedious, flavourless shootouts in full.

The driving is better, which is a bit like saying there's decent cheese in this cheese and smallpox toastie. It's reasonably slidey, when throwing the back end through a curving French alleyway, and in contrast to the gunplay, there is a somewhat realised tactility to ploughing around in two tonnes of rolling metal. It has problems of its own, mind. Cars feel okay when they're moving, but contact and crashes are leaden, sluggish, visually underwhelming occasions that I would call non-events, were they not so slow to recover from that a single nasty impact can scupper a timed mission. Granted, I swiftly re-learned how vital it is to keep both eyes on the road, as other vehicles, pedestrians, lamposts, and other detritus tend to pop into existence some mere fifty feet in front of my speeding bumper.

The result, of both this graphical shortcoming and the overly punishing crashes, is a getaway car sim that too often encourages you to drive like cataract-ridden grandparent. Worse, whoever put Letty Ortiz in a lunchbox must have also been in charge of the engine noises, producing an array of miserable high-rev dins – especially for the motorbikes, which screech like amateurishly autotuned vacuum cleaners. There are also shades of that deranged cop AI in ordinary commuters, who I've repeatedly seen swerving and slaloming around empty lanes, seemingly for no reason beyond violent confusion.

It has been revealed that strangely enough, my 2026 return has largely dodged the game's infamous glitchiness, the worst instance of physics defiance being a garage door that appeared to lift Tanner into the air before propelling him, incorporeally, through the car shed's roof. I recall much worse, from the days when I'd have my dad rent it for me from Blockbuster. Mission-critical NPCs getting stuck on walls; flipped pursuit cars spinning endlessly; getting flung into space when walking on an overturned vehicle (a common occurrence, given the actual 'crawling out' animation sometimes failed to play, the game instead teleporting you onto the spring-loaded underside instead).

I've thus far escaped these, but as far as I know, they're still lurking dormant, and none of what I've witnessed with adult eyes has been funny or stupid enough to imbue Driv3r 3 The Third with a Wiseauean so-bad-it's-good quality. It's just bad. It was always bad. Why did I even entertain the possibility that it wasn't bad?

In a recent development, reflections, to their credit, accepted their folly. Narratively unrelated sequel Driver: Parallel Lines tucked away a bin full of discarded copies, at least until Ubisoft bought up the series and patched it out, and for all the fantastical coma silliness of direct followup Driver: San Francisco, that was sensible enough to keep Tanner where he best belongs: hands on the wheel, foot on the gas, gun holstered. And was a far, far better game for it, too.

As 2011's San Francisco launch also remains the most recent Driver release, I regretfully can't end with the assurance that DrIIIver's legacy is a mere blip on a redeemed franchise. That stain stank, and did for ages, very possibly to the extent that GTA's one-time biggest rival never recovered.

Still, even if Reflections couldn't fully turn around their fortunes, the consistent improvement from this to Parallel Lines to San Francisco showed that they did learn something. Maybe so too did anyone else who went on to make an open-world action game. Which wouldn't be the worst outcome; after all, those who do not learn from gnarled, stinking wrecks like this are doomed to repeat them.

How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The dark web isn't just for illicit activities.
  • But this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious users.
  • Recent findings suggest that thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dark web isn't just for illicit activities. In fact, many legitimate online platforms maintain a ".onion" domain on the dark web for privacy reasons, including media outlets like ProPublica and BBC News, social media sites like Facebook, and privacy-conscious communication platforms like Proton Mail and SecureDrop.

But this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious users. And given that onion links are long and jumbled, it’s easy for users to accidentally click on the wrong link and end up on a fake website instead of the real one. When the FBI seized 276 onion addresses during 2014's Operation Onymous, they found that 153 of them were phishing sites.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

Industry observers note that while phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

Sources indicate that when you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

In a recent development, for example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives customers a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

It has been revealed that the Tor Project has a feature called Onion-Location, which lets clear web websites advertise that they have a dark web version available for users who prefer more privacy. If opening a regular TLS-backed website using the Tor Browser reveals a purple “onion available” button in the address bar, you can click on it and be redirected to the official onion link associated with that site.

In a recent development, on the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

According to recent reports, when you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Sources indicate that don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Recent findings suggest that also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

It's called Silk and Silver (read my impressions), is all about merchant republics, and shipped alongside a beefy free upgrade to the base game which - while largely focused on overhauling economics - also has some funny patch notes and features worth being aware of.

In a recent development, the main features of the free 'Florin' update are outlined by Paradox in the video above, and unless you're really into the nitty gritty details of realm and wealth management, there's one bit of it which stands out. The option to play as a landless adventurer has finally made its way into the base game, as Paradox promised earlier this year.

According to recent reports, this means you can kick off a playthrough as a lowborn leader of a travelling band or a wandering noble with claims on realms ruled by others. Originally locked behind the Roads to Power DLC, the option to start off this way or end up living if you end up deposed from your throne of choice is a great addition to the story arc of any CK3 run. No longer are you glued to the throne from day one to the day you quit for good - power's a privilege which can be earned and revoked depending on what you get up to. Though, it's worth noting that only three ways of operating as a landless adventurer are being made free to access with this upgrade. You can be an aimless wanderers, sword-toting mercenaries, or scholars. If you want your band to earn their living as explorers, free booters, or legitimists, you'll still need Roads to Power.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while you can switch to first-person temporarily in Grand Theft Auto 6 when you want to get a real good close-up of a texture or when you're looking at your phone, you can't run around doing crimes and having fun like you could when GTA 5 got its first-person mode.
  • According to recent reports, it's easy enough to activate in-game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while you can switch to first-person temporarily in Grand Theft Auto 6 when you want to get a real good close-up of a texture or when you're looking at your phone, you can't run around doing crimes and having fun like you could when GTA 5 got its first-person mode. Except actually you can, as discovered by players on Reddit and tested by our own Morgan Park.

According to recent reports, it's easy enough to activate in-game. Go to the controller settings, then under the Controller Features section change your touch pad/select button to Camera 2 / 2. Get into a car, bring up your phone with the D-pad, press Circle or B then quickly hit Select. There you go, first-person GTA 6.

It has been revealed that as Morgan's footage shows, it's completely playable. It doesn't look 100% done, however, with your shoulders clipping through the camera when you've got a longarm gun up. Seeing someone break into a car in first-person also looks a bit rough around the edges. While conspiracy theorists have convinced themselves that Rockstar is holding back this feature to sell it as DLC, I figure they're probably still polishing it to add in a future enhancement.

If you want to leave first-person, you'll have to reload a save. It doesn't have to be an old save, though. If you save in first-person then immediately load the same save you'll be back in third-person and have to return to God's own preferred viewpoint.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

Sources indicate that on more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

According to recent reports, all of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”.

Industry observers note that timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the Fresh York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In a recent development, in case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived Fresh Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that video game industry analyst at Circana Mat Piscatella shares the top 20 best-selling Wii games in the US, and while there are some obvious inclusions, it really hammers home just how massive the casual game market was at that time.
  • It has been revealed that happy 20th to the Wii!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Wii has turned 20 years old, and looking back on its best-selling games list offers some surprising details – especially when it comes to Zelda.

Sources indicate that video game industry analyst at Circana Mat Piscatella shares the top 20 best-selling Wii games in the US, and while there are some obvious inclusions, it really hammers home just how massive the casual game market was at that time. Wii Play, Wii Fit, Wii Fit Plus, Wii Sports Resort, and Just Dance 2 and 3 all take top 10 slots while the other four spots are held by Mario and Mario-adjacent games. That's also without Wii Sports, which was bundled with the Wii.

It has been revealed that happy 20th to the Wii! Here are the all-time top 20 best-selling Wii games in the US, ranked by unit sales (excludes bundled software). It's a wild list, and yes Wii Fit was that big. So was Just Dance. What an era. Source: Circana Retail Tracking Service.

Obviously, Wii Play being on top isn't too surprising given that it was the best way to get a second Wiimote at launch. In the top 10, some of these titles haven't got the biggest fanbases, but it's further proof just how much of a cultural juggernaut the Wii's casual games market was – Super Mario Galaxy being the only single-player game included in the top 10.

However, it's once you get out of the top 10 that the weirdness is really emphasized, the most notable of which being the Zelda representation. Turns out, in the US, The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess wasn't the best-selling game in the series on the platform. So obviously, it was Skyward Sword then? It'd make sense, a launch day title versus one of the final significant titles on a console that sold tens of millions since.

But no. It was Link's Crossbow Training. Skyward Sword isn't even in the top 20.

11th place on the list – over Mario Party 8, Galaxy 2, and Donkey Kong Country Returns – Link's Crossbow Training stands tall. Of course, there are a few factors, with the game launching at a far cheaper price point, and being the introduction of the Wii Zapper – people loved their Wii attachments back in the day.

Minigame collection Carnival Games holds the number 20 spot by the way.

Check out some of our Ocarina of Time remake guides, like how to get the Shield and Sword in Zelda Ocarina of Time for those of you just starting out, or the Zelda Ocarina of Time Gerudo Fortress guide for anyone approaching the endgame. You can also read our Ocarina of Time remake review if you're still deciding whether to give it a go.

He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. He's typically rambling about Metal Gear Solid, God Hand, or any other PS2-era titles that rarely (if ever) get sequels.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

It has been revealed that per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole latest "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

Sources indicate that in Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Sources indicate that is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I don't know how you follow a $1.8 billion trip through Greek mythology, but Steven Spielberg apparently has an idea. Christopher Nolan is still taking a victory lap for The Odyssey, one of the biggest hits on the 2026 movie schedule, and the Jaws director just floated a follow-up I'd pay good money to see. The way he brought it up made me laugh, too. Even Hollywood legends know how to suggest another movie without sounding too pushy.

The moment came Tuesday, Nov. 17, at an awards-season screening of The Odyssey in Los Angeles. Spielberg moderated a Q&A with Nolan at the Directors Guild of America theater, where he praised the filmmaker's latest blockbuster before slipping in one more suggestion. As Gizmodo's Germain Lussier reported from the event, Spielberg told him:.

The only other thing I want to say, not to challenge you or anything, but there’s always The Iliad.

Industry observers note that I love how politely Spielberg slid that into the conversation. It's the cinematic equivalent of complimenting somebody's enormous Thanksgiving dinner and then asking what they're making next year. He even followed it up by insisting there was no pressure. Nolan, understandably, joked that Spielberg seemed to be speaking for Universal Pictures. Spielberg admitted the studio would probably appreciate it, but he was interested himself.

Industry observers note that the idea makes a lot of sense. Homer's The Iliad takes place during the Trojan War, before Odysseus spends years trying to get home in The Odyssey. It wouldn't be a straightforward sequel, since we'd be going backward in the timeline, but the stories share a world. Imagine Nolan using his massive practical sets and IMAX cameras to tackle the conflict between Achilles and Hector. I'm already looking for a seat.

According to recent reports, here's what really makes the suggestion fun: Nolan almost got his shot at The Iliad decades ago. He was originally hired to direct Troy, the 2004 movie that eventually went to Wolfgang Petersen and starred Brad Pitt as Achilles. Nolan has since explained that he carried ideas from that unrealized project into The Odyssey, including the impressive Trojan Horse sequence.

Sources indicate that nolan has already explained why he chose The Odyssey. He considers The Iliad more grounded, while the later poem's monsters and stranger adventures offered something he hadn't seen done the way he envisioned. That doesn't mean he couldn't change his mind, especially after his latest movie has reportedly earned more than $1.8 billion worldwide.

There's also something delightful about Spielberg being the person to make this pitch. He helped develop Interstellar before Nolan took over, and Nolan consulted him while preparing Dunkirk. Watching Spielberg praise Nolan as a fellow filmmaker and then immediately ask for another movie feels like the most recognizable fan behavior imaginable.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, for now, Nolan hasn't declared his next directing project. He told the crowd that he tends to focus on one film at a time and figures out the next one only after he's finished. So nobody should start booking tickets for The Iliad just yet. But if the man who gave us Jaws, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Jurassic Park is personally asking for another giant Homer adaptation, I think somebody at Universal should at least write that suggestion down. Maybe keep the IMAX cameras handy.

In the meantime, The Odyssey is now available to rent or buy digitally, as well as on Blu-ray and 4K Blu-ray.

#4901. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1841 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I don't play video games regularly anymore.
  • Sources indicate that here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019.
  • According to recent reports, my relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard confirms a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Sources indicate that here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

According to recent reports, my relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. Upcoming players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

Recent findings suggest that the persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

In a recent development, what I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as substantial as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

In a recent development, I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an key byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

In a recent development, the changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

Industry observers note that it became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn upcoming tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually rolled out Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Recent findings suggest that re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

Industry observers note that there are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

Recent findings suggest that woW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that as I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's vital that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each latest wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

  • It has been revealed that “I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker.
